questions.stem: What is an electric current?
options: A flow of charge around a circuit
A store of energy in a battery
The heat produced by a lamp
questions.explanation: Current is charge in motion, measured in amperes.

questions.stem: What unit is current measured in?
questions.explanation: Amperes (amps) measure current. Volts measure voltage and ohms measure resistance.
questions.teaching:
Current is the rate at which charge flows past a point in a circuit, and like any rate it has its own unit.

That unit is named after André-Marie Ampère and is usually shortened to 'amps' in conversation. One of them means one coulomb of charge passing per second. It is measured with an ammeter connected in series — in line with the circuit — because the same charge has to flow through the meter as through the component. That contrasts with a voltmeter, which is connected across a component instead.

questions.stem: What unit is voltage measured in?
questions.explanation: Voltage is measured in volts and describes the energy given to each unit of charge.
questions.teaching:
Three core electrical quantities are constantly confused, so it helps to have a picture for each.

Think of a water circuit. The pressure pushing water round corresponds to the electrical push supplied by a cell or battery, measured in units named after Alessandro Volta. The rate of water flowing past a point corresponds to current, in amperes. And the narrowness of the pipe corresponds to resistance, in ohms. A voltmeter is connected across a component to measure the first, while an ammeter goes in line with the circuit to measure the second.

questions.stem: What does a battery do in a circuit?
options: Stores the current until it is needed
Provides the energy that pushes charge around the circuit
questions.explanation: The battery supplies energy. The charge is already in the wires — the battery does not create it.

questions.stem: What is a complete circuit?
options: A circuit with at least two lamps
A circuit with a switch in it
An unbroken conducting path from one terminal of the source to the other
Any wire connected to a battery
questions.explanation: Current only flows if the path is unbroken. A single wire attached at one end does nothing.

questions.stem: What does a switch do?
options: Opens or closes the circuit to stop or allow current
questions.explanation: An open switch breaks the path; a closed switch completes it.

questions.stem: What is resistance?
options: The energy supplied by a battery
The amount of charge in a wire
A measure of how much a component opposes current
questions.explanation: Higher resistance means less current for the same voltage. It is measured in ohms.

questions.stem: Which instrument measures current?
questions.explanation: An ammeter is connected in series to measure current through a component.
questions.teaching:
Two meters measure two different quantities, and they are connected to a circuit in two different ways.

The meter measuring the rate of flow of charge must have that same charge pass through it, so it is connected in series — cut the circuit and insert it in line. The meter measuring the electrical push across a component is connected in parallel, bridging across the component without breaking the circuit. Getting the connection wrong is the classic practical error, and the names tell you which quantity each one measures if you know the units.

questions.stem: Which instrument measures voltage?
questions.explanation: A voltmeter is connected in parallel across a component.
questions.teaching:
Meters are named after the quantity they measure, so knowing the units gives you the instrument names for free.

The quantity measured in volts describes the electrical push, or energy given to each unit of charge, and its meter is connected across a component in parallel — it compares two points, so it needs to touch both. The quantity measured in amperes describes the rate of charge flow, and its meter goes in series, in line with the circuit, so the charge passes through it. A multimeter can do both, but it has to be connected differently for each.

questions.stem: What is a conductor?
options: A material that lets current pass through easily
questions.explanation: Metals are good conductors because charge moves freely through them.

questions.stem: What is an insulator?
options: A material that does not let current pass through easily
questions.explanation: Plastic and rubber are insulators, which is why wires are coated in them.

questions.stem: In a series circuit, how are components connected?
options: In a circle with no source
One after another in a single loop
Side by side on separate branches
questions.explanation: Series means one path. Parallel means multiple branches.

questions.stem: In a parallel circuit, how are components connected?
options: On separate branches, each with its own path to the source
One after another in a single loop
questions.explanation: Each branch provides an independent path for current.

questions.stem: What happens in a series circuit if one lamp breaks?
options: The broken lamp is bypassed and the rest stay lit
questions.explanation: Breaking the single path stops all current, which is why old Christmas lights all failed at once.

questions.stem: What happens in a parallel circuit if one lamp breaks?
questions.explanation: Other branches still provide a complete path, which is why house wiring is parallel.

questions.stem: What is a fuse for?
options: Breaking the circuit if the current becomes too large
questions.explanation: A fuse melts and breaks the circuit, protecting against dangerous currents.

questions.stem: What does an LED do in a circuit?
options: Emits light when current flows through it in the correct direction
questions.explanation: LEDs only conduct one way, which is why they must be connected the right way round.

questions.stem: Which of these is a source of electrical energy in a circuit?
questions.explanation: Cells and batteries supply energy. Resistors, switches and lamps use or control it.
questions.teaching:
Every circuit needs something to supply energy to the charges, or nothing flows at all.

That role is filled by a chemical device that converts stored chemical energy into electrical energy, maintaining a potential difference across the circuit. Several of them joined together make a battery, strictly speaking, though the words are used interchangeably in everyday speech. Everything else in a circuit either uses that energy — lamps, motors, resistors — or controls its flow, like switches. So look for the component that supplies rather than consumes.

questions.stem: What happens to electrical energy in a lamp?
options: It is transformed into light and thermal energy
It is stored in the lamp
questions.explanation: A filament lamp produces far more heat than light, which is why LEDs are more efficient.

questions.stem: What is the symbol for a cell in a circuit diagram?
options: A long thin line and a short thick line
questions.explanation: A zigzag is a resistor and a circle with a cross is a lamp.

questions.stem: Why does adding more lamps in series make each one dimmer?
options: Each lamp blocks light from the others
The voltage of the battery increases
Total resistance rises, so current falls and each lamp gets less energy
questions.explanation: More resistance in one loop means less current for every component in it.

questions.stem: Why does household wiring use parallel rather than series connections?
options: Series wiring cannot carry enough current for large appliances
Parallel wiring reduces the total current drawn from the supply
Each appliance gets full voltage and can be switched independently
questions.explanation: Independent operation at full voltage is the practical requirement, and series cannot deliver it.

questions.stem: In a series circuit, how does the current compare at different points?
options: It is the same everywhere in the loop
It is largest nearest the battery
It gets used up as it passes each lamp
It is largest at the end
questions.explanation: Charge is not consumed. Energy is transferred, but the current is identical at every point in a series loop.

questions.stem: A student says the current is 'used up' by a lamp. What is the correction?
options: The current really is used up
Current only flows in one half of the circuit
Energy is transferred by the lamp, but the current is the same on both sides
questions.explanation: This is the most common circuit misconception. The lamp converts energy, not charge.

questions.stem: Why is a voltmeter connected in parallel with a component?
options: Connecting it in series would reverse its reading
It measures the current flowing through the component
It measures the potential difference — the energy transferred per unit of charge — across the component
It must carry the full current through itself to work
questions.explanation: Voltage is the energy carried per unit of charge between two points, so the meter must span those two points. An ammeter, which measures flow, goes in series instead.

questions.stem: Why is an ammeter connected in series?
options: The current being measured must pass through it
It measures voltage across a component
It would short out in series
questions.explanation: To count the flow, the meter must be in the flow's path.

questions.stem: What happens to the total resistance when identical resistors are added in parallel?
options: It decreases, because more paths are available for current
questions.explanation: More parallel routes make it easier for charge to flow overall, so total resistance falls.

questions.stem: Why do thin wires heat up more than thick ones carrying the same current?
options: A thin wire has higher resistance, so more energy is transferred as heat
questions.explanation: Resistance rises as cross-section falls, which is why undersized wiring is a fire hazard.

questions.stem: An LED is connected but does not light, and reversing it makes it work. Why?
options: An LED only conducts in one direction
The LED was faulty at first
The battery only works one way round
questions.explanation: LEDs are polarised components. Filament lamps work either way.

questions.stem: Which circuit change would make a lamp brighter?
questions.explanation: More voltage means more energy per charge and more current. Each other option increases resistance and dims it.

questions.stem: Why is a switch usually placed so it can isolate an appliance?
options: The switch converts energy to light
Opening the switch breaks the path and stops current safely
The switch reduces the voltage gradually
questions.explanation: A break in the conducting path is what makes the appliance safe to work on.

questions.stem: A circuit has a 6 V battery and two identical lamps in series. What is the voltage across each?
questions.explanation: The supply voltage divides across identical series components, so each gets half.

questions.stem: Why does the current in a parallel circuit split between branches?
options: Charge is created at each junction
Charge takes every available path, with more current through the branch of lower resistance
Charge chooses the shortest branch only
questions.explanation: Total current entering a junction equals the total leaving it. The split is inversely related to resistance: the easier path carries the larger share.

questions.stem: Why is it dangerous to overload a power board?
options: Total current rises, and wiring can overheat beyond its safe capacity
questions.explanation: Each device added in parallel increases total current, and the shared wiring has a limit.

questions.stem: Which evidence would best show that current is not consumed by a component?
options: Ammeters before and after a lamp reading the same value
The battery going flat over time
questions.explanation: Equal readings either side directly test the claim. The battery going flat shows energy transfer, not charge loss.

questions.stem: A torch dims as its battery ages. Explain in terms of voltage and current.
options: The lamp gains resistance over time
The current is used up by the switch
The charge in the wires runs out
The cell supplies less voltage, so less current flows and less energy reaches the lamp
questions.explanation: The chemical supply in the cell degrades, reducing the voltage available to drive current.

questions.stem: Why can a bird sit safely on a single high-voltage wire?
options: The wire has no current in it
Both feet are at nearly the same voltage, so almost no current flows through it
questions.explanation: Current needs a voltage difference. Touching a second wire or the ground would create one, with fatal results.

questions.stem: Two circuits use the same battery, one with lamps in series and one in parallel. Which drains the battery faster?
options: They drain at the same rate
The parallel circuit, because it draws more total current
The series circuit, because current passes through more lamps
questions.explanation: Lower total resistance means higher current and faster energy transfer, so the parallel circuit flattens the battery sooner.

questions.stem: Why is a circuit diagram more useful than a photograph of a circuit?
options: Standard symbols show the connections clearly regardless of physical layout
Diagrams show the true colours of the wires
questions.explanation: A diagram is a model: it strips away irrelevant physical detail so the electrical relationships are unambiguous.

questions.stem: What is a cell in electrical terms?
options: A single unit that supplies electrical energy from a chemical reaction
questions.explanation: Several cells joined together make a battery.

questions.stem: Which material is a good conductor?
questions.explanation: Metals conduct well; the other three are insulators.
questions.teaching:
Materials are classified by how easily charge moves through them, and the reason comes down to electrons.

In a conductor, some electrons are not bound to any one atom and are free to drift through the material, so charge flows easily. Metals are the standard example, and a few are used constantly in wiring because they combine good conduction with reasonable cost and ductility. In an insulator, electrons are tightly held, so almost no charge flows — plastic, rubber, glass and dry wood. That is exactly why a wire is one material wrapped in the other.

questions.stem: What does a resistor do in a circuit?
options: Reduces the current by opposing its flow
questions.explanation: Resistors are used deliberately to control current.

questions.stem: What is a short circuit?
options: A low-resistance path that lets a very large current flow
A circuit that is too small
A circuit with a broken wire
questions.explanation: Short circuits can cause dangerous heating, which is why fuses exist.

questions.stem: What happens when a switch is open?
options: The circuit is broken and no current flows
questions.explanation: An open switch creates a gap in the conducting path.

questions.stem: What is a circuit diagram?
options: A drawing using standard symbols to show how a circuit is connected
A graph of current over time
questions.explanation: Standard symbols make the connections unambiguous regardless of physical layout.

questions.stem: What does a variable resistor allow you to do?
options: Change the resistance and so control the current
Change the voltage of the battery
questions.explanation: A dimmer switch is a common everyday example.

questions.stem: Why are wires coated in plastic?
options: Plastic is an insulator and prevents accidental contact
questions.explanation: The insulation keeps current in the wire and people safe.

questions.stem: What is the difference between a cell and a battery?
options: A cell is larger than a battery
A battery is two or more cells joined together
questions.explanation: In everyday speech the words are used interchangeably, but technically a battery is a set of cells.

questions.stem: Which component protects a circuit by melting if the current is too high?
questions.explanation: The fuse is a deliberate weak point that breaks the circuit safely.
questions.teaching:
Circuits need protection because too much current generates heat, and heat in wiring causes fires.

The simplest protective component is a deliberately weak link: a thin piece of wire designed to be the first thing to overheat. If the current climbs past a set value, it melts, breaking the circuit and stopping the flow. It has to be replaced afterwards, which is the downside. A circuit breaker does the same job with a switch that trips and can be reset, which is why modern switchboards use them instead.

questions.stem: Two cells are connected in series instead of one. What is the effect on a lamp?
options: It becomes brighter because the voltage is higher
questions.explanation: Series cells add their voltages, driving more current through the lamp.

questions.stem: Why does a circuit with a short circuit across a lamp leave the lamp unlit?
options: Current takes the low-resistance path around the lamp
questions.explanation: Most of the current bypasses the lamp through the near-zero resistance path.

questions.stem: In a parallel circuit, how does the total current compare to each branch current?
options: Total current equals the sum of the branch currents
Total current equals one branch current
Total current is less than any branch
questions.explanation: Charge is conserved at junctions, so what enters equals what leaves.

questions.stem: Why does a car headlight circuit use thick wires?
options: Thin wires cannot carry any current
Large currents need low resistance to avoid overheating
questions.explanation: Resistance falls as cross-sectional area rises, limiting heat generated.

questions.stem: Why is a voltmeter designed to have very high resistance?
options: So it can carry the full current
So it draws almost no current and does not alter the circuit it measures
questions.explanation: A measuring instrument should disturb the system as little as possible.

questions.stem: Why is an ammeter designed to have very low resistance?
options: So it can measure voltage too
So inserting it barely changes the current it is measuring
questions.explanation: Adding significant resistance in series would reduce the very current being measured.

questions.stem: What happens to the brightness of lamps in series when one is replaced with a higher-resistance lamp?
options: The current rises to compensate for the added resistance
All lamps dim, because total resistance rises and current falls
questions.explanation: In series the same current flows everywhere, so a change affects all components.

questions.stem: Why does a torch stop working if a battery is inserted the wrong way in a two-cell torch?
options: The bulb filament conducts in one direction only
The reversed cell recharges the other one
The cells oppose each other, so the net voltage is near zero
questions.explanation: Opposing cells cancel, leaving little or no driving voltage.

questions.stem: Why does connecting a voltmeter in series with a lamp cause the lamp to go out?
options: The voltmeter's very high resistance reduces the current to almost nothing
The voltmeter stores all the charge
questions.explanation: This is a common wiring error, and the symptom follows directly from the meter's design.

questions.stem: Why is mains electricity distributed at high voltage over long distances?
options: Higher voltage pushes charge along the wires faster, so less is lost on the way
Higher voltage lowers the resistance of the cables, so less energy becomes heat
Higher voltage lets thinner cables carry the same current without overheating
Higher voltage means lower current for the same power, reducing energy lost as heat in the wires
questions.explanation: Losses depend strongly on current, so reducing current reduces waste.

questions.stem: Two circuits have the same battery. Circuit A has one lamp, circuit B has two in series. Compare battery life.
options: Circuit A drains the battery faster because it draws more current
They drain at the same rate
questions.explanation: Lower total resistance in A means higher current and faster energy transfer.

questions.stem: Which evidence would best show that a circuit fault is a break rather than a short?
options: The battery becomes very hot quickly
No current flows anywhere and the battery does not get warm
questions.explanation: A break stops all current; a short produces a large current and rapid heating.

questions.stem: Why does adding a resistor in series reduce a lamp's brightness but adding one in parallel does not?
options: A parallel resistor shares the current evenly with the lamp, which keeps the lamp's share constant
A series resistor reduces the current through the lamp; a parallel one provides a separate path
A series resistor lowers the supply voltage, while a parallel one leaves the supply voltage unchanged
A series resistor is closer to the lamp in the loop, so more of the energy is lost before it arrives
questions.explanation: The lamp keeps its full voltage in the parallel case, so its current is unchanged.

questions.stem: Why is it misleading to say electricity 'flows out' of a power point into an appliance?
options: Current requires a complete loop, so charge flows around the circuit and back
Electricity does not move at all
Charge is consumed by the appliance
questions.explanation: A circuit is a loop. Energy is transferred to the appliance, but charge circulates rather than being delivered one way.

questions.stem: What is a series circuit's defining feature?
options: There is only one path for the current
questions.explanation: One path means the same current flows through every component.

questions.stem: What component would you use to control a lamp's brightness smoothly?
questions.explanation: A switch is on or off; a variable resistor allows gradual control.

questions.stem: What is an electrical insulator used for in a plug?
questions.explanation: The plastic casing keeps the conducting parts isolated.

questions.stem: What is a filament in a lamp?
options: A thin wire that heats and glows when current flows
questions.explanation: Its high resistance causes it to heat until it emits light.

questions.stem: What does a circuit need in order for current to flow?
options: A complete conducting path and a source of voltage
questions.explanation: Both a driving voltage and an unbroken loop are required.

questions.stem: What is a parallel circuit's defining feature?
options: Components are on separate branches with their own paths
All components share a single path
questions.explanation: Each branch operates independently.

questions.stem: What happens to charge as it passes through a lamp?
options: It continues on, having transferred energy
questions.explanation: Energy is transferred, but the charge itself continues around the loop.

questions.stem: Which unit measures resistance?
questions.explanation: Resistance is measured in ohms, using the Greek letter omega as its symbol.
questions.teaching:
Electrical quantities each have their own unit, and matching quantity to unit is the fastest way through these questions.

The push driving charge around a circuit is measured in one unit. The rate of flow of charge is measured in another. The opposition to that flow — how hard a component makes it for charge to get through — is measured in a third, named after Georg Ohm and written with a Greek letter. The three are linked by Ohm's law, so knowing any two gives the third. Power, in watts, is a fourth quantity again.

questions.stem: Two lamps in series, one rated higher resistance. Which is brighter?
options: The higher-resistance lamp, because more energy is transferred in it
questions.explanation: With the same current, more resistance means more energy transferred per second.

questions.stem: Why do household appliances have an earth wire?
options: It provides a safe path for current if a fault makes the casing live
questions.explanation: The earth wire protects users by carrying fault current safely away.

questions.stem: What is the effect of adding a third cell in series to a two-cell circuit?
options: The voltage increases, so more current flows
The current stays the same, with each cell supplying less
questions.explanation: Series cells add their voltages.

questions.stem: Why does a battery become warm during use?
options: The wires push heat into it
Its internal resistance converts some energy to heat
It absorbs heat from the air
questions.explanation: No source is perfectly efficient; some energy is lost inside the cell.

questions.stem: Which arrangement would let two lamps be switched independently?
options: A single loop with no switch
Parallel branches each with its own switch
questions.explanation: Independent operation requires separate paths and separate switches.

questions.stem: Why does a circuit diagram place the ammeter symbol in the main loop?
options: An ammeter must be in series to measure the current flowing
questions.explanation: Current must pass through the meter to be counted.

questions.stem: Why can a fuse rated too high fail to protect a circuit?
options: It will not melt until the current is already dangerously large
questions.explanation: The rating must match the circuit's safe current, not simply be large.

questions.stem: Why does a voltmeter across a battery read slightly less when a large current flows?
options: The meter draws current and so lowers its own reading
Some voltage is dropped across the battery's internal resistance
questions.explanation: Terminal voltage falls below the cell's full value under load.

questions.stem: Why are parallel circuits used in a house rather than series?
options: Series wiring cannot carry enough current for large appliances
Parallel branches share the supply voltage between them
Each appliance receives the full supply voltage and works independently of the others
Parallel wiring draws less total current than series
questions.explanation: In series, switching one appliance off would cut power to everything.

questions.stem: A circuit's total resistance falls when a branch is added. Explain.
options: An extra path gives charge more routes, so overall opposition decreases
questions.explanation: This is why total current rises when parallel branches are added.

questions.stem: Why is it dangerous to replace a fuse with a piece of ordinary wire?
options: The wire will not melt at a safe current, so the circuit loses its protection
questions.explanation: Removing the deliberate weak point allows dangerous currents and overheating.

questions.stem: A student measures 0.3 A in one branch and 0.5 A in another of a parallel circuit. What is the current from the battery?
questions.explanation: Branch currents sum to the total leaving the source.

questions.stem: Why is high resistance desirable in a voltmeter but not in connecting wires?
options: A voltmeter must not divert current, while wires must carry it with minimal energy loss
Both should match the resistance of the component
questions.explanation: Each component's resistance is chosen for the job it must do.
